items.title: Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 are 40 percent off ahead of Black Friday
items.summary: AirPods Pro 3 | Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge The AirPods Pro 3 are cheaper than ever. Apple’s latest flagship wireless earbuds dropped this morning to just $149 at Amazon and Walmart . Originally, they sold for $249, but have been commonly available for $199 outside the range of deal events. The best price that we’ve previously seen was $169, which is what they’re currently selling for at Best Buy. It’s a weird situation that, right now, the feature-packed AirPods Pro 3 are the same price as the newer (but less impressive) AirPods 5 that include the wireless charging case. The Pro 3 deliver considerably more bang for your buck. AirPods Pro 3 Where to Buy: $249 $149 at Amazon $249 $149 at Walmart $249 $169.99 at Best Buy This model is Apple’s best-sounding, longest-lasting AirPods, and they ship with five silicone ear tips. Compared to the second-gen AirPod Pro, these offer better water resistance (IP57 versus IP54), longer battery life per charge (eight hours versus six), improved noise cancellation, and heart rate sensing through built-in sensors. The case also has Apple’s second-gen Ultra Wideband chip in the case. Read our AirPods Pro 3 review.

Why long distances, fast-moving satellites, and Doppler shift challenge the physical layer, including synchronization, timing advance, and HARQ operation. How mobility works in NTN, including cell selection, conditional handover, feeder link switchover, and movement between terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks. How to test NTN devices, satellites, and networks with RF, protocol, and over-the-air methods under realistic fading and propagation conditions. How NTN evolves toward 6G unified networks that combine multiple bands, layers, and dimensions, with sensing, positioning, and AI. Download this free whitepaper now!

items.author: Andrew Herrick
items.title: A job that changed me: My last shift as a truck driver was nearly done. Then a man shouted ‘You’re on fire!’
items.summary: I was 22 and didn’t have a heavy vehicle licence. But I was game, in that ‘I’ll-do-anything-once’ kind of way I only got the job because my boss was desperate. It was peak sales season, November 1978. Our factory in bayside Melbourne had run radio ads featuring an actor pretending to be a burglar boasting how easy it was to rob places that didn’t have our security doors. People wanted their houses fortified for the holidays. Stock requests were flooding in from stores around the city. Our truckie – let’s call him Kelvin – a corpulent alcoholic with a Chopper moustache, had just been jailed for evading road tax. The firm’s accountant, who’d agreed to fill in, wasn’t fit to drive. He coached the local men’s football team and his wife had just run off with its champion goal-kicker.

items.originalTitle: Beneath Its Brilliant Surface, Blade Runner 2099 Lacks a Human Soul
items.author: Judy Berman
items.title: Beneath Its Brilliant Surface, Blade Runner 2099 Lacks a Human Soul
items.summary: Michelle Yeoh in Blade Runner 2099 —Clay Enos—Prime For nearly half a century, the Blade Runner franchise has been on the run from the accusation that its future-noir visual style eclipses the substance of its stories. Critics rhapsodized over the look of Ridley Scott’s 1982 film—a box-office flop that gradually achieved cult-classic status on home video—but judged it to be, as Janet Maslin wrote in the New York Times , “a mess, at least as far as its narrative is concerned.” TIME’s Richard Corliss concluded that “ Blade Runner , like its setting, is a beautiful, deadly organism that devours life.” Denis Villeneuve ’s 2017 sequel, Blade Runner 2049 , fared somewhat better in theaters and with reviewers, though the critiques were of a similar nature. In the years since I took in that 164-minute epic on the biggest screen available, those hazy, saffron-tinted, almost tangibly toxic landscape shots of a bombed-out wasteland that used to be Las Vegas have stayed with me more than the busy plot. That its mise-en-scène is more memorable than its storytelling may strike Blade Runner’s most devoted audience as a feature, not a bug. When movies attract cult followings, it’s usually the immersive vibe that keeps fans coming back. Television is a different medium, though, one that can be greatly enhanced by technical artistry but needs to be anchored in a compelling narrative and characters with depth in order to hold our attention episode after episode. The speculative worlds of sci-fi TV must be as intricately constructed as they are aesthetically awesome. Prime Video’s Blade Runner 2099 , an eight-part limited series that will stream in full on Nov. 25, never quite overcomes its big-screen legacy. Its visual ambition is astounding. Yet that bleak beauty continues to obscure the personalities of its protagonists and the shape of their society. From left: Lewis Gribben, Hunter Schafer, and Dimitri Abold in Blade Runner 2099 —Clay Enos—Prime As its title suggests, 2099 takes place a few generations after 2049 . Maybe because the environmental and corporatocratic dystopia of the original Blade Runner ’s then-near-future, now-recent-past 2019 Los Angeles was becoming hard to distinguish from our reality, showrunner Silka Luisa ( Shining Girls ) adds a major dread-enhancing development. Once enslaved to build “Off-world” colonies for refugees of an increasingly uninhabitable Earth, replicants—the flesh-and-blood humanoids engineered by the monolithic Tyrell Corporation to be “more human than human,” i.e., smarter, stronger, and 20 times more productive than us—have overthrown their inferior masters. Now, as they endeavor to restore the global ecosystem, humanity is the underclass relegated to grunt work. Of course, not every human submits. Rebels assume false identities to fight their oppressors. And just as earlier installments followed LAPD officers called blade runners, who are tasked with killing rogue replicants, this one centers around a unit of Los Angeles replicant cops rooting out rogue humans. Confusingly but perhaps necessarily, given the franchise’s branding, they’ve appropriated the blade runner moniker. Olwen is one such blade runner, now just days away from the preordained death date with which all replicants are born; that this character is played by Michelle Yeoh , who at 64 has lost none of her action-star prowess, is its own implicit argument against planned obsolescence. As she attempts to stay stoic about her demise, she’s partnered with Cora ( Hunter Schafer ), a human fugitive protecting her disabled younger brother, Elias (Lewis Gribben). Cora's desperate circumstances have driven her to go undercover as a blade runner. It isn’t easy for a human to impersonate a replicant. While the subtle differences in appearance can be faked, replicants aren’t just superior to humans by every quantifiable metric—they also supposedly lack empathy, a side effect of being gestated to adulthood in artificial wombs rather than raised by loving parents. Michelle Yeoh, left, and Hunter Schafer in Blade Runner 2099 —Clay Enos—Prime As tends to be the case in odd-couple, buddy-cop stories, Cora and Olwen have more in common than they know. A draconian spoiler list prevents me from getting too specific about their joint quests, but suffice to say that the human’s rough past has equipped her to blend in with her taciturn new colleagues and the replicant has a greater capacity for interpersonal connection that she realizes. Schafer and Yeoh come from very different onscreen backgrounds (while Yeoh earned global fame as the queen of Hong Kong action movies, Schafer is best known for her arresting work as the artistic love interest of Zendaya’s character in HBO’s lurid and downbeat Euphoria ), but both excel at layering vulnerability beneath a stolid mask. This is not the most creative premise. Even so, it could’ve made an adequate foundation for a show that really engaged viewers—who are still predominantly human, I’m told—with Cora, Olwen, the mostly underwritten characters around them, the relationships among all of the above, and the overlapping societies in which they’re situated. The texture of everyday human life in L.A., such as it is under the boot of the Übermenschen humanity created, doesn’t get much attention. Nor do we understand the larger philosophies or motivations or social structures of the replicants, who can’t reproduce sexually and for whom “ongoing relationships” are proscribed. A peepshow-esque establishment where physically optimized replicants try on prosthetics like pregnant bellies and saggy, elderly skin offers the most telling glimpse at their fantasy lives. These are the details great sci-fi shows like Andor and The Expanse are built on. Here, they’re few and far between. Our understanding is, for the most part, limited to the goals that drive Olwen and Cora and various villains in their hunts for particular objects and people—video-game stuff. (Would it shock you to learn that the owners of this IP do indeed envision video games in its future?) Part of the problem is how little 2099 shows us of the relationships these characters are so invested in. Rather than replicants who are more human than human, we get humans who, in the mootness of their personalities, are more replicant than replicant. Screen time that might’ve been spent on narrative world-building is instead given over to aesthetic world-building. For all that it lingers on eye candy long enough to induce a sugar coma, the series really does look incredible. Production designers Paul Inglis and Chloe Arbiture, working with huge art and effects teams, have done a spectacular job expanding on Blade Runner ’s seedy, cyberpunk cityscapes and the glowing desolation of 2049 . There are imposing corporate interiors of classical proportions, massive brutalist complexes reclaimed by nature, abandoned metropolises whose arched, white buildings recall the eerie tableaus of Giorgio de Chirico . Human slums are grubby and cramped but irrepressibly colorful. This is all far easier to do than it was 44 years ago, yet the sheer number of vividly rendered settings and the fact that the series looks so much more real than the typical Marvel VFX job makes it a true technical achievement. If these visuals are destined to be repurposed as backdrops for some big-budget, open-world Blade Runner video game, then 2099 will be a gift to gamers most of all.
